name: Late Iron Age
caption: Rome holds the Mediterranean, Gaul and Hispania. Beyond the Rhine and the Danube live Germanic, Baltic, Slavic and Sarmatian peoples that Roman writers know only by report. Celtic languages are spoken from Ireland to the Danube.

name: Roman period
caption: Rome rules from Hadrian’s Wall to the Black Sea. Inside the frontier the peoples keep their names as districts and Latin and Greek spread. Outside it, Tacitus and Ptolemy name the Germans, Balts and Sarmatians.

name: After Rome
caption: The names stop; the people do not. Roman rule ends in the west. Goths, Franks, Lombards and others become the rulers of Latin speakers, which is what the stripes show. Huns hold the Danube plain for a lifetime.

name: Early kingdoms
caption: Slavic speakers spread across the east, the centre and the Balkans. Franks rule Gaul, Visigoths Hispania, Lombards Italy, and Avars the Danube plain. Constantinople holds Greece and the coasts.

name: Conquest and Carolingians
caption: Muslim armies take most of Hispania. Charlemagne’s Franks rule from the Ebro to the Elbe. Bulgars found a state on the Danube, and Norse raids begin in 793.

name: Viking age
caption: The Frankish empire divides. Magyars settle the Danube plain in 895. Norse found states from Dublin to Kiev. Poland, Bohemia, Hungary, Denmark, Norway, Sweden and Rus take up Christianity and enter the written record.

name: High Middle Ages
caption: Normans take England and Sicily. Christian kingdoms take most of al-Andalus. German settlers move east. The Mongols destroy Kievan Rus in 1240 and hold the steppe.

name: Late Middle Ages
caption: The Ottomans cross into Europe in 1354 and take Constantinople in 1453. Moscow gathers the Rus lands. Poland and Lithuania unite. Granada falls in 1492.

name: Early modern
caption: Ottoman rule reaches Hungary. Spain, France, England, Sweden and Russia grow into large states, and national languages spread at the cost of their neighbours.

name: Age of nations
caption: Empires and then nations. Poland is partitioned, Italy and Germany unite, and the Balkan states leave the Ottoman empire. Schools, armies and print carry national languages into every village.

name: Since 1922
caption: The borders of 1919, 1945 and 1991. War, expulsion and resettlement after 1939 made language areas match state borders more closely than at any earlier time. The full build draws this century from census tables.

name: Rome and Parthia
caption: Rome holds Anatolia, Syria and Egypt, and Parthia holds Mesopotamia. Most people speak Greek, Aramaic or Egyptian. Arab kingdoms trade from Petra to Yemen. Strabo, Pliny, Josephus and thousands of inscriptions give the names.

name: Rome and the Sasanians
caption: Two empires fight over Armenia and Mesopotamia, each with Arab allies, the Ghassanids and the Lakhmids. Armenia and Georgia become Christian and gain alphabets. Himyar unites Yemen. Syriac and Armenian chronicles join the Greek ones.

name: Arab conquests
caption: Armies from Arabia take Syria, Iraq and Egypt within ten years. Umayyad caliphs rule from Damascus. The conquered still speak Aramaic, Coptic and Greek. The record is Arabic history written a century or two later.

name: Abbasid centuries
caption: Baghdad is the seat of the Abbasid caliphs. Arabic spreads from the garrison towns to the villages of Syria, Iraq and Egypt. Byzantium keeps Anatolia, Armenian and Georgian kingdoms revive, and the Fatimids take Egypt in 969.

name: Turks and Crusaders
caption: Seljuk Turks defeat Byzantium at Manzikert in 1071 and Turkish speakers settle the Anatolian plateau. Crusaders hold the Levant coast from 1099. Saladin's Ayyubids rule Egypt and Syria, and Georgia is at its height.

name: Mongols and Mamluks
caption: Mongols sack Baghdad in 1258 and are stopped in Palestine in 1260. Mamluks rule Egypt and Syria. Anatolia divides among Turkish beyliks, one of which becomes the Ottoman Empire. Coptic and most Aramaic give way to Arabic.

name: Ottomans and Safavids
caption: The Ottomans take Syria, Egypt and Iraq. Their frontier with Safavid Persia runs through Kurdistan, Armenia and Georgia. Tax registers list villages by faith. Zaydi imams hold Yemen, and Omani imams the south-east.

name: Empires in retreat
caption: Egypt goes its own way under Muhammad Ali and is occupied by Britain in 1882. Russia takes the Caucasus. Saudi emirs rise in Najd. In 1915 the Armenians of Anatolia are deported and killed.

name: Nation states
caption: Mandates and then independent states divide the Ottoman lands. Greeks leave Anatolia in 1923. Israel is founded in 1948 and Hebrew is spoken again. Kurds live in four states. The status of the Palestinian territories is disputed.

name: Roman Africa
caption: Rome rules the coast from Egypt to Morocco. Berber is spoken everywhere west of the Nile, with Punic and Latin in and around the towns of Tunisia. The Garamantes hold the Fezzan. Pliny, Ptolemy and inscriptions give the names.

name: Vandals and Byzantines
caption: Vandals take Carthage in 439 and Constantinople takes it back in 533. Moorish kings rule the interior, some using Latin. Egypt speaks Coptic under Greek-speaking governors. Procopius and Corippus are the main witnesses.

name: Arab conquest
caption: Arab armies take Egypt in 641 and Carthage in 698. Kairouan and Fez are Arabic-speaking towns in a Berber countryside. Berbers adopt Islam, often in dissenting forms, and found states at Tahert and Sijilmasa.

name: Fatimids and Zirids
caption: The Fatimids rise among the Kutama Berbers, take Egypt in 969 and found Cairo. Zirid Berbers govern Ifriqiya for them. Ibn Hawqal and al-Bakri describe the towns and peoples of the Maghreb and the Sahara.

name: Berber empires
caption: Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym Bedouin move west from Egypt, and Arabic spreads across the plains. Almoravids from the Sahara and then Almohads from the Atlas unite the Maghreb and al-Andalus. Coptic is fading in Egypt.

name: Three kingdoms
caption: Marinids at Fez, Zayyanids at Tlemcen and Hafsids at Tunis divide the Maghreb, and Mamluks rule Egypt. Berber holds the mountains and the Sahara. Ibn Khaldun writes their history. Castile conquers the Canary Islands.

name: Ottoman regencies
caption: Ottoman governors and corsair captains rule Algiers, Tunis and Tripoli, and Egypt is an Ottoman province. Morocco stays independent under Saadi and then Alaouite sharifs. Tuareg confederations control the Saharan roads.

name: Colonial rule
caption: France takes Algiers in 1830, Tunisia in 1881 and most of Morocco in 1912. Britain occupies Egypt in 1882 and Italy invades Libya in 1911. Colonial surveys map Arabic and Berber speech for the first time.

name: Independence
caption: Morocco, Tunisia, Algeria, Libya and Egypt are independent states. Arabic is the main language everywhere, and Tamazight is also official in Morocco and Algeria. Sovereignty over Western Sahara is disputed.

name: 1 to 250
caption: Rome and Han China hold the two ends of Eurasia, with Parthia and the Kushans between. Bantu-speaking farmers are moving through eastern Africa. Maya cities carve dated monuments. Polynesia beyond Samoa, Madagascar and New Zealand have no people yet.

name: 250 to 600
caption: Steppe peoples press on every settled empire. Rome falls in the west and China divides. The Guptas rule north India and Aksum the Red Sea. Teotihuacan and the Classic Maya flourish. Farming and iron reach southern Africa.

name: 600 to 900
caption: Arab armies carry Islam and Arabic from Spain to the Indus. Tang China and the Tibetan empire face Turks and Uyghurs. Srivijaya rules the straits. Sailors from Borneo settle Madagascar. Wari and Tiwanaku hold the Andes.

name: 900 to 1200
caption: Turkic peoples move into Iran and Anatolia. Song China, the Cholas and Angkor prosper. Ghana and Kanem trade across the Sahara. Polynesians reach the eastern Pacific, Norse reach Greenland, and Thule Inuit cross the Arctic. Cahokia rises on the Mississippi.

name: 1200 to 1500
caption: The Mongols conquer from Korea to Hungary, and their empire divides. Mali and then Songhai rule the Sahel, Great Zimbabwe the plateau. Polynesians settle Hawaii, Rapa Nui and New Zealand, the last large lands. The Mexica and the Inca build empires.

name: 1500 to 1750
caption: Europeans cross the oceans. Disease and conquest empty much of the Americas, and Spanish, Portuguese, English and French take root there. Ottomans, Safavids, Mughals, Ming and Qing rule most of Asia. The Atlantic slave trade grows. Russia crosses Siberia.

name: 1750 to 1900
caption: Empires of Europe take India, Australia, most of Africa and the Pacific. The United States and the new republics of Latin America spread across their continents. Native languages lose ground everywhere settlers arrive. Qing China doubles in size, then weakens.

name: 1900 to now
caption: The empires break up into nearly two hundred states. Schools, cities and broadcasting spread a few dozen national languages at the cost of thousands of small ones. The map now rests on censuses, though many count languages poorly.

name: Han, Kushan and Parthian
caption: Han China, the Kushans, Parthia and the Satavahanas are known from their own records. The Xiongnu and other steppe peoples are known from Chinese accounts. Southeast Asia and Siberia are known mostly from archaeology and later languages.

name: Division and the Guptas
caption: China divides between northern dynasties founded by steppe peoples and Chinese dynasties in the south. The Guptas rule north India and the Sasanians Iran. Turks appear on the Altai. Funan and the first Indian-style kingdoms arise in Southeast Asia.

name: Tang, Tibet and the Caliphate
caption: Tang China, the Tibetan empire, the Turk and Uyghur khaganates and the Arab caliphate meet in Central Asia. Arabic spreads over the Near East. Srivijaya and Java's kingdoms rule the islands, Nara Japan and Silla Korea take up Chinese writing.

name: Song, Cholas and Seljuks
caption: Song China is ringed by the Khitan, Tangut and Jurchen states. Turks rule from Anatolia to north India and take up Persian. The Cholas raid Sumatra. Angkor and Pagan are at their height. Tai speakers are moving south.

name: The Mongol century
caption: Mongol armies take China, Iran, Central Asia and the Rus lands, then the empire divides into four. Delhi's sultans hold north India. Tai kingdoms replace Angkor's rule. Majapahit dominates the islands.

name: Ming, Mughals and Safavids
caption: Ming and then Qing China, Mughal India, Safavid Iran and the Ottomans rule most of Asia. Islam spreads through the islands. Russians cross Siberia to the Pacific by 1640. Portuguese, Dutch and English traders hold ports.

name: Empires from outside
caption: Britain takes India and Burma, France Indochina, the Dutch the Indies, and Russia Central Asia. Qing China conquers the Dzungars and Tibet, then loses ground. Japan modernises and builds an empire of its own.

name: Since independence
caption: New states replace the empires. National languages such as Mandarin, Hindi, Indonesian and Russian spread through schooling, and many hill and forest languages shrink. Several borders are disputed and the map does not settle them.

name: Early towns and villages
caption: Evidence is archaeology, except Maya inscriptions. Teotihuacan grows in Mexico, Moche and Nazca on the Peruvian coast, Hopewell mounds in Ohio. Language areas are projected back from much later.

name: Classic period
caption: Maya city states carve dated monuments. Teotihuacan falls about 600. Tiwanaku and Wari rule the Andes. Arawakan farmers settle the Greater Antilles. Outside the Maya lowlands everything rests on archaeology.

name: Tula, Chimor and Cahokia
caption: Toltec Tula, Chimu Chan Chan and Cahokia on the Mississippi are the great towns. Norse farm in Greenland from 985. Tupi speakers hold the Brazilian coast. Evidence is archaeology and later tradition.

name: Mexica and Inca
caption: Thule Inuit spread from Alaska to Greenland. Athabaskan speakers move south. The Mexica and the Inca build empires known from histories written down after the conquest. Elsewhere, archaeology and oral tradition.

name: Conquest and epidemics
caption: Spain takes the Caribbean, Mexico and Peru. Smallpox and other diseases kill most people in many regions. European writers now name hundreds of peoples, often after great losses.

name: Colonial empires
caption: Spanish, Portuguese, English, French and Dutch colonies hold coasts and highlands. Most of North America, the Amazon and the far south remain native. Haudenosaunee, Mapuche and Pueblo peoples fight the newcomers.

name: Horses and frontiers
caption: Horses remake the Plains and the Pampas. Comanche, Lakota and Mapuche expand. Fur traders reach the Rockies and Russians reach Alaska. Colonial languages still cover a minority of the land.

name: Independence
caption: The United States, Haiti, the Spanish American republics and Brazil become independent. Most of the western interior of North America, the Amazon, the Chaco and Patagonia are still native country.

name: Removal and settlement
caption: Eastern nations are removed west. Railways, armies and settlers take the Plains, the Pampas, Araucania and Patagonia. Canada forms in 1867. Native languages retreat to reserves, forests and the Arctic.

name: Since 1900
caption: Spanish, English, Portuguese and French cover most of the map. Quechua, Aymara, Guaraní, Mayan languages, Nahuatl, Navajo, Cree and Inuit languages are still widely spoken, and Amazonia keeps hundreds of small languages.

name: Meroe and early Aksum
caption: Rome holds Egypt and the northern coast. Kush rules the middle Nile from Meroe and Aksum rises in the Horn. Bantu-speaking farmers have reached the Great Lakes. Khoe and San hold the south. South of the Sahara the evidence is mostly archaeology.

name: Aksum and Christian Nubia
caption: Aksum is Christian and at its height. Nobatia, Makuria and Alwa follow Kush on the Nile. Vandals, then Constantinople, hold the northern coast. Ironworking Bantu farmers spread through East Africa and south past the Limpopo, known from their pottery.

name: Arab conquest and Ghana
caption: Arab armies take Egypt from 640 and the Maghreb by 710, and the Fatimids rise there. Arab writers begin to describe Ghana, Gao, Kanem and the Zanj coast, where Swahili towns grow. Nubia stays Christian.

name: Almoravids, Ife and Zagwe
caption: Almoravids and then Almohads rule the Maghreb, and Ghana fades. Kanem turns to Islam. Zagwe kings build Lalibela's churches. Ife casts its bronzes. Mapungubwe grows rich on gold and ivory traded to the Swahili coast.

name: Mali and Great Zimbabwe
caption: Mali rules the western Sahel and Mansa Musa's pilgrimage makes it famous. Mamluks hold Egypt. Kilwa and Great Zimbabwe prosper. Solomonic kings rule Ethiopia. Arabic spreads up the Nile as Christian Nubia ends. Portuguese ships reach the coasts after 1440.

name: Songhai, Kongo and the Oromo
caption: Songhai rules the Niger bend until Morocco's invasion of 1591. The Ottomans take Egypt and most of the Maghreb. Oromo spread over southern Ethiopia. Portugal deals with Kongo, Benin and Mutapa. Bornu and the Funj hold the central Sahel and the Nile.

name: Atlantic trade
caption: The Atlantic slave trade peaks. Asante, Dahomey and Oyo grow strong on the Guinea coast, Luba and Lunda in the savanna, Buganda by the lake. Dutch settlers spread from the Cape over Khoekhoe land. Ottoman regencies rule the northern coast.

name: Jihads and Mfecane
caption: Fula reformers found Sokoto, Massina and the Tukulor empire. Zulu wars scatter Nguni and Sotho peoples as far as Tanzania. Boers trek inland. Zanzibar's traders reach the Congo. Egypt conquers the Sudan and France takes Algiers.

name: Colonial partition
caption: Between 1880 and 1912 European powers divide almost the whole continent, north and south of the Sahara. Ethiopia and Liberia stay independent. The borders drawn then cut across peoples and languages, and most of them still stand.

name: Independent states
caption: Most colonies become states between 1956 and 1975, Namibia in 1990 and South Sudan in 2011. Arabic fills the north. Hausa, Swahili, Amharic and the colonial languages spread as common tongues. Some borders remain disputed.

name: Iron Age and first ports
caption: Mon, Khmer and related languages fill the mainland lowlands, Pyu towns stand on the Irrawaddy, and Austronesian speakers hold the islands and the Cham coast. Evidence is archaeology, later languages, and brief notices in Chinese, Greek and Indian texts.

name: Funan and first inscriptions
caption: Funan on the lower Mekong and Champa on the coast appear in Chinese histories. Sanskrit inscriptions begin from Vietnam to Borneo and Java. The Red River delta is a Chinese province. Most peoples are still known only from archaeology.

name: Srivijaya and Chenla
caption: Srivijaya at Palembang commands the straits, and the Sailendras build Borobudur in Java. Chenla, Mon Dvaravati and the Pyu cities share the mainland. Inscriptions now use Old Khmer, Old Malay, Old Javanese, Cham and Mon.

name: Angkor, Pagan and Dai Viet
caption: Angkor rules from the Mekong to the Chao Phraya. Burmese speakers found Pagan and take the Mon south. The Viet throw off Chinese rule in 939 and press on Champa. Kediri and Singhasari follow Mataram in Java.

name: Tai kingdoms and Majapahit
caption: Tai speakers found Sukhothai, Lan Na, Lan Xang and Ayutthaya on old Mon and Khmer ground, and Angkor declines. Majapahit dominates the islands. Islam takes root at Pasai and then Malacca.

name: Sultanates and spice trade
caption: Malacca, Aceh, Brunei, Demak, Ternate and Gowa spread Islam along the trade routes. Dai Viet takes most of Champa in 1471. Portuguese, Spanish and Dutch arrive, and Spain holds Manila from 1571. Toungoo Burma briefly rules the mainland.

name: Burma, Siam and Vietnam
caption: Three large kingdoms take shape. Konbaung Burma conquers the Mon, Siam recovers at Bangkok after 1767, and the Vietnamese settle the Mekong delta. The Dutch company controls Java and the spice islands, and Spain the lowland Philippines.

name: Colonial rule
caption: Britain takes Burma and Malaya, France Indochina, the Dutch the whole archipelago, and the United States the Philippines in 1898. Siam alone stays independent. Chinese and Indian migrants settle the ports. Japan occupies the region from 1941 to 1945.

name: Independent states
caption: Independence comes between 1945 and 1984, and Timor-Leste follows in 2002. National languages such as Indonesian, Thai, Burmese, Vietnamese and Filipino spread through schools, while several hundred local languages are still spoken, many by shrinking communities.

name: The western Pacific
caption: Australia and New Guinea have been peopled for some fifty thousand years and hold hundreds of languages. Descendants of the Lapita voyagers live in island Melanesia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, and Micronesia is settled. All of this is known from archaeology and languages.

name: Into eastern Polynesia
caption: After a long pause in Tonga and Samoa, canoes reach the Cook, Society and Marquesas Islands around 1000 to 1100. Radiocarbon dates, shared words and oral tradition are the evidence, and the dates are debated. Madagascar, far to the west, is already settled.

name: Hawaii, Rapa Nui, Aotearoa
caption: Within about a century voyagers settle Hawaii, Rapa Nui and, around 1280, Aotearoa New Zealand, the last large lands on Earth to be peopled. Sweet potato from South America shows that some canoes reached that coast and returned.

name: Island chiefdoms
caption: Long voyages become rarer and each island group goes its own way. The Tu'i Tonga receive tribute from Samoa to Fiji, Hawaiian chiefs build large estates, Rapa Nui raises its moai, and Māori build fortified pā. Genealogies recorded later are the main source.

name: First European sightings
caption: Magellan crosses in 1521 and Spain occupies Guam and the Marianas in 1668, with heavy loss of Chamorro life. Mendaña, Quirós, Tasman and Roggeveen sight islands and sail on. For most islanders life is still recorded only by tradition and archaeology.

name: Cook, missions and kingdoms
caption: Wallis, Bougainville and Cook chart the islands and write the first long accounts. Introduced diseases cut populations sharply. Missionaries arrive from 1797, and chiefs with firearms unite Hawaii, Tahiti and Tonga as kingdoms. Britain settles Australia from 1788.

name: Colonial Pacific
caption: Britain, France, Germany and the United States divide the islands. Settlers take most land in New Zealand, Hawaii and New Caledonia, and Indian labourers come to Fiji. English and French spread. Only Tonga keeps its own monarchy throughout.

name: Independence and revival
caption: Samoa leads independence in 1962 and most island groups follow by 1980, while some remain with France, the United States or New Zealand. Māori, Hawaiian and other languages are taught again, and voyaging canoes sail the old routes.

name: Parthians and Kushans
caption: Parthian kings rule Iran and the Kushans rise in Bactria. Sogdians and Khwarezmians farm the oases, and Saka and Sarmatian herders hold the steppe. The evidence is Greek and Chinese report and coins, so steppe positions are loose.

name: Sasanians and Huns
caption: Persian Sasanians rule the plateau. Kidarite and Hephthalite Huns take Bactria and Sogd. On the steppe Iranian speech gives way to peoples whose languages are unknown. Inscriptions, coins and Sogdian and Bactrian documents survive.

name: Turks and Arabs
caption: Turkic khaganates take the steppe and overlordship of the oases after 552. Arab armies end the Sasanian empire in 651 and reach Samarkand by 712. Chinese, Arabic and Sogdian records overlap for the first time.

name: Samanids and the Persian revival
caption: Persian-speaking Muslim dynasties rule from Bukhara, Nishapur and Rayy, and New Persian replaces Sogdian and Bactrian. Oghuz, Karluks and Kimeks hold the steppe, Bulgars and Khazars the Volga. Turkic Kara-Khanids and Ghaznavids divide the Samanid lands in 999.

name: Seljuks and Khwarazmshahs
caption: Oghuz Turks under the Seljuks conquer Iran, and Turkic speech spreads into Azerbaijan and the Karakum. Kipchaks hold the steppe from the Irtysh to the Volga. Kara-Khitai, Ghurids and Khwarazmshahs divide the east.

name: Mongol khanates
caption: Chinggis Khan destroys the cities of Transoxiana and Khurasan from 1219. His heirs rule as the Ilkhans in Iran, the Chagatai khans in the oases and the Golden Horde on the steppe. Within a century they speak Turkic or Persian.

name: Timurids and the new hordes
caption: Timur and his heirs rule from Samarkand and Herat. The Golden Horde breaks into Kazan, Sibir, the Nogai, the Uzbeks and the Kazakhs. Turkmen confederations hold western Iran.

name: Safavids and Uzbek khanates
caption: Safavid shahs make Iran Shia. Uzbek khans rule Bukhara and Khiva, Kazakhs the steppe, and Dzungars press on them from the east. Russia takes Kazan, Astrakhan and Sibir and builds forts across Siberia.

name: Russian conquest
caption: Durrani Pashtuns found Afghanistan and Qajars reunite Iran. Russia takes the Kazakh steppe by the 1840s and Tashkent, Samarkand and the Turkmen oases between 1865 and 1884. The census of 1897 counts the empire by language.

name: Soviet republics and nation states
caption: Moscow divides Central Asia into republics named for nations in 1924 and settles many Russians in the north. The five republics become independent in 1991. Iran has been an Islamic republic since 1979, and Afghanistan has been at war since 1978.

name: Satavahanas and Kushans
caption: Prakrit is spoken across the north, Dravidian languages in the south, Munda and Gondi in the central hills. Kushans hold the north-west, Satavahanas the Deccan, and Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas the Tamil coast. Coins, inscriptions and Greek traders are the evidence.

name: Gupta age
caption: The Guptas rule the Ganges plain and their allies the Vakatakas the Deccan. Pallavas and Kadambas rise in the south. Sanskrit inscriptions and the pilgrim Faxian describe the north. Huna invaders break the empire after 480.

name: Harsha and the Chalukyas
caption: Harsha rules the north from Kannauj and the Chalukyas of Badami hold the Deccan against him. Pallavas and Pandyas divide the Tamil country. Xuanzang describes each kingdom. Arabs conquer Sindh in 712.

name: Three empires
caption: Palas of Bengal, Pratiharas of the west and Rashtrakutas of the Deccan fight for Kannauj. Rajput clans appear. The eastern Prakrits spread across Bengal and Assam, and Kannada and Telugu become written languages.

name: Cholas and Rajputs
caption: The Cholas hold the south and northern Sri Lanka. Rajput kingdoms divide the north while Ghaznavid and then Ghurid armies come through Punjab. Hindi, Bengali, Marathi and the other modern languages begin to be written.

name: Sultanates and Vijayanagara
caption: The Delhi Sultanate conquers the north and raids the south, then breaks into regional sultanates. Vijayanagara holds the south against the Bahmanis. Ahoms settle Assam, Pashtuns the Peshawar valley, and a Tamil kingdom rules northern Sri Lanka.

name: Mughal Empire
caption: The Mughals bring nearly all of India under one Persian-writing court. Rajput kings serve them. Portuguese, Dutch and English traders hold ports. Nepali spreads east through the hills and Kandy keeps the interior of Sri Lanka.

name: Successor states and the Company
caption: Marathas, Sikhs, the Nizam, Mysore and the nawabs of Bengal and Awadh divide the Mughal lands. Gorkha unites Nepal. The East India Company takes Bengal in 1765 and by 1849 rules or controls all of India.

name: British India
caption: The crown rules the provinces and oversees hundreds of princely states. Censuses from 1881 and Grierson's survey record languages village by village. Hindi and the other plains languages keep spreading into the Munda and Gondi hills.

name: Independent states
caption: Partition in 1947 creates India and Pakistan and moves millions across Punjab and Bengal. Bangladesh separates in 1971. India redraws its states by language. Sovereignty over Kashmir remains disputed.

name: Han and Xiongnu
caption: The Han empire rules Chinese speakers on the Yellow River and Yangzi, with Yue, Tai and other peoples across the south. Xiongnu then Xianbei hold Mongolia. Chinese histories are almost the only written evidence, and name the Wa and the Korean Han.

name: Division
caption: China divides. Xiongnu, Xianbei, Di and Qiang leaders found states in the north and Chinese migrants move south of the Yangzi. Rouran then Turks rule the steppe. Goguryeo, Baekje, Silla and Yamato take shape.

name: Sui, Tang and Tibet
caption: Sui and Tang reunite China. A Tibetan empire holds the plateau, Nanzhao holds Yunnan, and Turks then Uyghurs hold Mongolia. Silla unites Korea, Balhae rules Manchuria, and Japan's court state pushes north against the Emishi.

name: Song, Liao and Jin
caption: Song rules a China growing fast in the south. Khitan Liao, Tangut Xia and Jurchen Jin take the north. Uyghur Turkic replaces Tocharian and Saka in the Tarim oases. Goryeo rules Korea and warriors take power in Japan.

name: Mongol empire
caption: Chinggis Khan unites the steppe in 1206. His heirs conquer Xia, Jin, Dali and Song, and rule China as the Yuan. Goryeo and Tibet submit. Japan turns back two invasions.

name: Ming and its neighbours
caption: Ming rules China and settles garrisons in Yunnan and Guizhou. Mongols and Oirats hold the steppe, Jurchens Manchuria. Joseon reaches the Yalu and Tumen. Japan is divided among warring lords, and Ryukyu trades across the seas.

name: Qing expansion
caption: The Manchu Qing take China, then Mongolia, Tibet, Dzungaria and the Tarim. Chinese settlers fill the south-western hills. Russia reaches the Pacific, and its records first name the peoples of eastern Siberia. Tokugawa Japan is at peace.

name: Empires and revolution
caption: Chinese farmers settle Manchuria and Inner Mongolia, Russians the Amur, Japanese Hokkaido. Japan builds an empire over Korea and Manchuria that ends in 1945. The Qing fall in 1912, and Mongolia breaks away.

name: Since 1949
caption: The People's Republic of China, Mongolia, two Korean states and Japan. Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Russian now cover almost all the ground, with Tibetan, Uyghur and Mongolian the largest of the other languages. Census figures replace estimates.

name: Before any writing
caption: No writing exists. Archaeology shows people in both lands for fifty thousand years. Pama-Nyungan languages cover most of Australia, the dingo is present, and New Guinea highlanders have farmed for millennia. Named peoples are projected back from later records.

name: Old countries
caption: Known only from archaeology, languages and oral tradition. Camps grow larger, eel traps are worked at Budj Bim, and Western Desert speech spreads across the arid west. Oceanic-speaking sailors trade along New Guinea's coasts and islands.

name: First sails
caption: Tidore claims tribute from the Bird's Head coast. Jansz meets people on Cape York in 1606, Torres passes the strait, and Tasman sights Tasmania in 1642. The written record is a few ships' journals and touches only the shore.

name: Sweet potato and trepang
caption: Sweet potato reaches the New Guinea highlands and populations grow, as oral histories recall. Makassan fleets visit Arnhem Land each year for trepang and trade with Yolŋu. Cook charts the east coast in 1770. Inland, evidence remains archaeology and tradition.

name: Invasion of the south-east
caption: Britain founds Sydney in 1788. Smallpox, sheep and guns take the south-east and Tasmania, and peoples resist in frontier wars. First Fleet journals, explorers and protectors now name peoples. Elsewhere, countries are still known only to their owners.

name: Frontier and colonies
caption: Six colonies spread across Australia and violence follows the pastoral frontier north and west. Missions and reserves begin. Germany, Britain and the Netherlands divide New Guinea but hold only its coasts. Tok Pisin grows on the plantations.

name: Federation and patrols
caption: Australia federates in 1901 and governs Papua and, from 1914, German New Guinea. Protection laws control Aboriginal lives and remove children. In 1933 patrols meet hundreds of thousands of farmers in the New Guinea highlands. War crosses the island in 1942.

name: Rights and independence
caption: Indonesia takes over Dutch New Guinea in 1963, which many Papuans contest. Gurindji walk off Wave Hill in 1966 and the 1967 referendum counts Aboriginal people in the Commonwealth. Papua New Guinea becomes independent in 1975.

name: Land rights and today
caption: The Mabo judgment of 1992 recognises native title, and determinations now cover much of Australia. English dominates, yet desert, Arnhem Land and Torres Strait languages are still spoken. Papua New Guinea keeps over 800 languages. West Papua's status remains contested.
